item.title: Committee questions $18.5m retained funds with M-Paisa and MyCash
item.description: The Standing Committee on Public Accounts has raised concerns over more than $18.5 million in unused funds that remained with M-Paisa and MyCash after the completion of a government program, with auditors unable to sight documentary evidence authorising the retention. In its review report on the Compliance Audit Report, the committee noted that $18,511,428 remained with the two service providers f
item.content:encoded:
The Standing Committee on Public Accounts has raised concerns over more than $18.5 million in unused funds that remained with M-Paisa and MyCash after the completion of a government program, with auditors unable to sight documentary evidence authorising the retention.

In its review report on the Compliance Audit Report, the committee noted that $18,511,428 remained with the two service providers following the completion of the programs, namely the COVID-19 Cash Assistance Program and the Food Ration Distribution Program.

The Ministry of Finance informed auditors that the Permanent Secretary had approved retaining the money for future initiatives.

However, the audit found that documentary evidence supporting that approval could not be sighted.

The committee said the situation raised concerns about transparency and compliance with financial management requirements.

It recommended that formal documentary approval be maintained whenever government funds are retained in service provider accounts after the completion of a program.

“Ensure unutilized balances are either promptly returned to the Consolidated Fund or formally reallocated with clear authorization,” the committee recommended.

The committee also stressed the need for stronger procedures governing the management of public funds, particularly during emergency or unpredictable situations.

“The Committee further emphasizes the importance of developing clear guidelines, procedures, and protocols to address future unpredictable events,” the report stated.

It said structured frameworks should be established covering risk assessments, documentation requirements and digital verification.

“Establishing structured frameworks for risk assessment, documentation standards, and digital verification mechanisms will ensure that emergency responses are not only swift but also transparent, accountable, and resilient,” the committee said.

The findings highlight the committee’s push for a clear audit trail when unused government funds remain outside the Consolidated Fund following the completion of publicly funded programs.

item.title: Millions paid to insurance company, but few benefited – Kiran
item.description: Government decided to end its welfare insurance scheme after determining that only $33.8 million of about $60 million spent on the program reached beneficiaries through direct insurance payouts, Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran told Parliament last week. Speaking on the cessation of the welfare insurance scheme, Ms Kiran said the figures showed the insurance model was
item.content:encoded:
Government decided to end its welfare insurance scheme after determining that only $33.8 million of about $60 million spent on the program reached beneficiaries through direct insurance payouts, Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran told Parliament last week.

Speaking on the cessation of the welfare insurance scheme, Ms Kiran said the figures showed the insurance model was an inefficient way of delivering assistance to vulnerable Fijians.

“Out of that $60 million, only $33.8 million actually reached our citizens as direct payouts,” she said.

Ms Kiran said in the 2023-2024 financial year, Government paid $7.1 million in insurance premiums while claims totalled $3.8 million.

In 2024-2025, premiums increased to $7.2 million, but claims again amounted to $3.8 million.

For the 2025-2026 financial year, she said $7.7 million was paid in premiums while only $3 million was paid out in claims.

“On average, a mere 56 percent of the total funds paid out by the government ended up in the hands of the beneficiaries,” Ms Kiran said.

“The remaining 44 percent did not serve our poor. Instead, it was absorbed by administrative friction, overheads and private corporate margins.”

She told Parliament no responsible government could regard the loss of 44 per cent of welfare funding through the delivery mechanism as economically sustainable.

“In macroeconomics, we call this a deadweight loss to our public finances,” she said.

Ms Kiran said Government had been spending about $7 million annually to provide insurance coverage for approximately 100,000 welfare recipients.

However, she said the insurance framework had processed an average of only about 5,000 claims annually over the past five years.

“We are paying massive premium blocks for a system where 95 percent of the covered population see no tangible touchpoint or benefit in any given year,” she said.

Ms Kiran said the figures demonstrated why Government could no longer justify continuing with the existing welfare insurance arrangement.

item.title: PAC audit report flags 12,602 duplicate COVID Payments
item.description: More than 12,000 duplicate payments worth $630,100 were made during the second round of Fiji’s COVID-19 Cash Assistance Program, according to findings highlighted in the Compliance Audit Report. The Standing Committee on Public Accounts, in reviewing the report, noted that auditors identified 12,602 duplicate payments in Round 2 of the assistance program.
item.content:encoded:
More than 12,000 duplicate payments worth $630,100 were made during the second round of Fiji’s COVID-19 Cash Assistance Program, according to findings highlighted in the Compliance Audit Report.

The Standing Committee on Public Accounts, in reviewing the report, noted that auditors identified 12,602 duplicate payments in Round 2 of the assistance program.

While recovery processes were subsequently introduced in Round 3, the report found that 62 duplicate payments worth $3,100 remained unrecovered, pointing to continuing weaknesses in payment controls.

The committee has called for stronger system controls to prevent duplicate applications and payments.

It also recommended authorities “ensure full recovery of overpayments and maintain transparent reporting of recovery actions.”

Concerns were also raised about reconciliation processes for cash disbursements.

According to the report, reconciliations did not contain documented sign-offs from those preparing and reviewing them.

This meant auditors could not confirm that the reconciliations had been independently prepared and reviewed within the required timeframe.

The committee recommended that documented sign-offs by preparers and reviewers be mandatory for all reconciliations to demonstrate independent preparation and timely review.

The findings relate to the COVID-19 Cash Assistance Program, which was delivered over five rounds and distributed more than $226 million in assistance.

Round 1 provided $90 each to 118,000 applicants, while recipients in Rounds 2 and 3 received $50 each.

Payments increased substantially in the final two rounds, with eligible recipients receiving $360 each.

Round 4 covered 294,924 recipients and distributed about $105.7 million, while Round 5 provided assistance to 241,347 applicants, with approximately $87.5 million distributed.

Overall, more than one million applicant payments were recorded across the five rounds as Government progressively expanded financial support during the COVID-19 period.

item.title: 23-year-old hands himself in over Nadi taxi robbery
item.description: A 23-year-old man has handed himself over to Police in connection with the aggravated robbery of a taxi driver iniNadi this morning. The suspect surrendered this evening and is currently being questioned at the Lautoka Police Station.
item.content:encoded:
A 23-year-old man has handed himself over to Police in connection with the aggravated robbery of a taxi driver iniNadi this morning.

The suspect surrendered this evening and is currently being questioned at the Lautoka Police Station.

The robbery occurred at around 8am and was captured on the taxi’s dash camera. The video, which has since gone viral, shows the taxi driver pleading for his life during the attack.

Assistant Commissioner of Police Operations Kasiano Vusonilawe said the Western Division Taskforce was continuing its search for the other suspects allegedly involved.

ACP Vusonilawe said Police were intensifying operations to apprehend those involved in robberies and burglaries and ensure they are brought to justice.

He condemned the attacks on innocent people who work hard to earn a living, describing the incidents as cowardly attacks on people who have made personal sacrifices to provide for themselves and their families.

item.title: Government relaxes tourism tax rules
item.description: The Government has relaxed the application of its new Tourism Services Tax, confirming that the five per cent levy will now apply only to new bookings made from September 1, 2026. The decision means tourists who booked their Fiji holidays before September 1 will not have to pay the new tax, even if they travel and use tourism services after the tax takes effect.
item.content:encoded:
The Government has relaxed the application of its new Tourism Services Tax, confirming that the five per cent levy will now apply only to new bookings made from September 1, 2026.

The decision means tourists who booked their Fiji holidays before September 1 will not have to pay the new tax, even if they travel and use tourism services after the tax takes effect.

The Government announced the change following discussions involving the Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Tourism and Civil Aviation and the Tourism Action Group.

“Bookings made before 1 September 2026 will not be subject to TST, even where the tourism service is provided after that date,” the Government said.

“This provides certainty for visitors and enables tourism operators to honour existing bookings and contractual arrangements.”

The concession represents a significant change in the implementation of the tax following concerns from sections of the tourism industry over its application to existing bookings.

The Tourism Services Tax will still take effect on September 1 and apply to qualifying tourism operators and services under the Tourism Services Tax Act 2026.

It will remain in place until August 31, 2027.

Government said the revised transition arrangement recognised the importance of tourism to Fiji’s economy.

“This practical transition reflects the Government’s recognition of tourism’s vital contribution to Fiji’s economy, employment, businesses and communities,” the statement said.

“It also demonstrates the Government’s commitment to listening to the industry and working collaboratively on policies that support sustainable economic growth.”

The announcement comes amid strong industry concerns about visitors being charged an additional five per cent on holidays they had already booked, and in some cases paid for, before the tax was announced.

The Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association had specifically called on Government to exempt existing bookings, arguing that visitors should not face an additional charge they could not have anticipated when making their travel arrangements.

Government has now effectively adopted that position, drawing a clear line between bookings made before September 1 and new bookings made from that date.

The Fiji Revenue and Customs Service will issue updated guidance and work with tourism stakeholders ahead of implementation.

Government also thanked tourism operators and workers for their contribution to the industry and acknowledged visitors from Australia, New Zealand and other international markets for continuing to choose Fiji.

“Fiji remains open, welcoming and ready to share its renowned hospitality with the world,” the Government said.

item.title: Ledua, Rokotunidau cases adjourned
item.description: The cases of Isaia Ledua and Saimoni Rokotunidau have been adjourned to September 10. In the first case, Justice Tuiqereqere cancelled a bench warrant against Mr Ledua after he presented himself in court this afternoon.
item.content:encoded:
The cases of Isaia Ledua and Saimoni Rokotunidau have been adjourned to September 10.

In the first case, Justice Tuiqereqere cancelled a bench warrant against Mr Ledua after he presented himself in court this afternoon.

Explaining his non-appearance at 9.30am today, Mr Ledua told the court he had contacted his lawyer, Jerry Dinati, in the morning, who had informed him that they would attend court together.

Justice Tuiqereqere reminded Mr Ledua of the consequences of failing to comply with the court’s orders.

Mr Ledua faces one count each of aggravated burglary and damaging property.

He is alleged to have committed the offences with others between April 7 and 9 this year and allegedly damaged an armoury keypad locker valued at $730.

In a separate matter before the same judge, the court heard that Mr Rokotunidau has been an inpatient at hospital since his last appearance in court while in custody.

Mr Dinati, who also represents Mr Rokotunidau, has been directed to advise his client on his plea.

Mr Rokotunidau faces one count each of attempted murder, unlawful possession of illicit drugs, going equipped for theft, serious assault, and refusing to have his fingerprints and photographs taken.

The matter was adjourned to September 10.

item.title: Tourism body challenges Government over new tax
item.description: The Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association has rejected Government claims that the tourism industry is using “delaying tactics” and risks “sabotaging” the Tourism Services Tax, saying its concerns are focused on protecting visitors who booked their holidays before the new levy was announced. FHTA chief executive officer Fantasha Lockington said the association supported Government assistance for Fiji
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association has rejected Government claims that the tourism industry is using “delaying tactics” and risks “sabotaging” the Tourism Services Tax, saying its concerns are focused on protecting visitors who booked their holidays before the new levy was announced.

FHTA chief executive officer Fantasha Lockington said the association supported Government assistance for Fiji Airways and was not calling for the five per cent tax to be scrapped.

However, she said applying the tax to bookings made and paid for before its introduction was unfair to visitors and risked damaging Fiji’s reputation as a tourism destination.

“Put yourself in the position of a family in Australia or New Zealand who booked and paid for their Fiji holiday eight months ago,” Ms Lockington said.

“They budgeted for a set price, in good faith, based on the rules that existed at the time. They now arrive to find an unexpected charge added to their bill, for a tax that didn’t exist when they booked.”

She said the dispute was not about whether Fiji Airways deserved support, but about the treatment of existing bookings.

“This isn’t a debate about whether Fiji Airways deserves support. It’s about Government going back on what it told this industry it would do and then refused to provide the consumer fairness the tax called for.”

FHTA said it had sought an assurance during consultations that bookings already contracted, and in many cases fully paid, would be exempt from the levy.

According to the association, that assurance was initially provided but was subsequently overturned in the final legislation and guidance without explanation.

FHTA also challenged Government’s reference to tourism contributing about five per cent of corporate tax collected nationally.

It argued that corporate tax reflected profits rather than the industry’s overall economic contribution, pointing to Government’s own figures that tourism generated about 40 per cent of Fiji’s economic activity and nearly $3 billion in foreign exchange earnings annually.

The association said members were already experiencing the impact of the tax, including at least one confirmed case involving a multi-room group booking that was cancelled and rebooked to another destination because of the additional charge.

“Every cancelled booking is a passenger who was going to fly Fiji Airways to get here, and now won’t,” Ms Lockington said.

“We want Fiji Airways to succeed. But applying this tax retrospectively to bookings that were already locked in gives visitors a reason to cancel rather than a reason to fly here. That helps no one, least of all the airline.”

FHTA also distanced itself from recent comments attributed to the Tourism Action Group supporting the tax, saying it withdrew from TAG on July 4, 2026, and that the group’s positions no longer represented FHTA’s views.

Ms Lockington said FHTA’s request remained for Government to exempt bookings made and paid for before the tax was announced.

“We support what Government is trying to do for Fiji Airways,” she said.

“We are simply asking Government to keep its word on how this would apply to people who had already booked their holiday. That is not too much to ask.”

item.title: ‘Look out for one another’
item.description: CHARITY, compassion and concern for others should be practised every day rather than reserved for religious occasions, says Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica. Speaking at the National Milad-un-Nabi Jalsa 2026 at Churchill Park in Lautoka yesterday, Mr Kamikamica said the life and teachings commemorated during Milad-un-Nabi offered practical lessons for Fiji’s communities.
item.content:encoded:
CHARITY, compassion and concern for others should be practised every day rather than reserved for religious occasions, says Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica.

Speaking at the National Milad-un-Nabi Jalsa 2026 at Churchill Park in Lautoka yesterday, Mr Kamikamica said the life and teachings commemorated during Milad-un-Nabi offered practical lessons for Fiji’s communities.

He said these values should extend beyond religious teachings and be reflected in people’s daily interactions.

“The first lesson is compassion,” he said.

Mr Kamikamica said people should show mercy and kindness to vulnerable, poor and suffering members of society.

He urged Fijians to look out for one another, including checking on struggling neighbours, showing patience towards colleagues and giving their time and resources to those in need.

He said honesty and integrity were equally important, particularly in maintaining trust within institutions, organisations and relationships.

“No institution, organisation and no relationship of trust can be sustained without this quality.”

Mr Kamikamica also highlighted humility as an important lesson, saying leadership and service should not be measured by status.

“The Prophet’s life was marked by simplicity and humility.”

He said the fourth lesson, unity, was particularly relevant to Fiji’s multicultural society.

Mr Kamikamica said the Prophet’s example demonstrated how people from different backgrounds could come together through shared values and mutual respect.

He said this reflected the Fiji the country was building, one where people of different communities, cultures and faiths could see themselves first and foremost as Fijians.

“We are bound together by respect, decency and a shared future.”

Mr Kamikamica said the fifth lesson was service to humanity, stressing that faith should be demonstrated through actions and the way people treated others.

He said the values of compassion, integrity, humility, unity and service should guide people beyond religious celebrations and become part of everyday life.
